speaker: Patrick Collison
question: In software engineering tooling, what major architectural idea from older programming environments like Smalltalk or Lisp machines is still missing from mainstream code editors?
guest: I think the basic idea of a true development environment and not just a text editor is really the right idea, and that's the thing I want to see a return to. That's the thing that the Lisp machines had in Genera, that Mathematica has to some extent, and that Smalltalk has. I think it's just such a mistake that we have ended up with development environments where there is such a separation between the text editing, the runtime, and the environment in which the code runs. Those are three slightly conceptually different things, and in those older environments, they can all coexist in the same place. Still to this day, I use Mathematica a lot, not because I'm doing arcane symbolic mathematics, but because it's just a more efficient development environment. VS Code has been a step slightly in that direction, but we could take it way further. What I'd love to see, for example, is when I hover over a line of code, I see profiling information about the runtime characteristics of that code or function, plus logging and error information overlaid. When I hover over a variable, I'd like to see the most common values that it takes on in production—those kinds of rich, deep integrations.

points.core: Mainstream tools mistakenly separate text editing from the live execution runtime.
points.note: Accept: decoupling static code editors from the runtime or execution environment; treating IDEs as text editors rather than unified live environments (as in Smalltalk, Lisp machines, or Mathematica). Do not credit: generic complaints about slow IDEs or praise of autocomplete.

points.core: Editors should overlay live runtime profiling metrics directly onto source lines.
points.note: Accept: inline performance telemetry, execution latency, resource usage, or live error and logging overlays shown directly on lines or functions in the editor. Do not credit: generic advice to use external APM dashboards or add print statements.

points.core: Inspecting a variable in code should reveal its typical production values.
points.note: Accept: hovering over or inspecting variables in the editor to view common, observed, or sampled runtime/production value distributions. Do not credit: static type annotations alone or standard local breakpoint debugging.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
The biggest missing idea is the **live, image-based environment**: the editor, the language runtime, and your running program are one and the same system, rather than separate tools exchanging text files.

In Smalltalk or on a Lisp machine, you didn't edit dead source text, then compile, launch, and attach a debugger. You worked inside a running world of live objects. You could inspect any object, change a method while the program ran, and see the effect immediately. When an error occurred, the debugger opened at the point of failure, and you could fix the code and resume execution from that frame without restarting. The whole system, including the tools themselves, was written in the same language and modifiable from within, and its state persisted as an image.

Mainstream editors like VS Code remain fundamentally text-file manipulators that talk to external processes through protocols such as LSP and DAP. Hot reload, REPLs, and notebooks recover fragments of the experience, but the core architecture, where code is treated as living structured objects rather than files, with no boundary between editing and running, has never become mainstream.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer:
Mainstream code editors are still missing image-based, live runtime integration—the architectural idea that the editor, compiler, debugger, and running application should coexist inside a single persistent, reflective environment rather than operating on static text files stored on disk.

In Smalltalk and Lisp machines, there was no boundary between writing code and running a program, nor between the development tools and the software being built. Developers interacted directly with live program structures in memory rather than dead source text: redefining a method or function mutated the running system in place without restarting a process or losing application state, and unhandled errors opened a live debugger where code could be repaired and execution resumed from the exact point of failure. Because the environment itself was constructed from the same inspectable objects and runtime primitives as user code, developers could also inspect and reshape their own tools on the fly. Modern editors, by contrast, remain fundamentally file-centric text processors communicating at arm's length with external build pipelines, language servers, and disposable OS processes.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
The biggest missing idea is the **live, image-based environment**. In Smalltalk and on Lisp machines, the editor, debugger, compiler and your running program all lived in one persistent world of live objects. Code wasn't mainly a set of dead text files that get compiled and launched separately. You could inspect any running object, change a method while the program was paused in the debugger, and resume. The tools themselves were written in the same language, and you could change them while they ran. They could also ask the running system directly about things like senders, implementers and the class hierarchy, without guessing from source text.

Mainstream editors like VS Code and JetBrains IDEs still treat programs as text files. Services like the Language Server Protocol rebuild structure from that text from the outside, and the program runs in a separate process the editor mostly can't see into. Hot reload, Jupyter notebooks, Clojure REPLs, Emacs and Pharo's Glamorous Toolkit recover pieces of this, but none is mainstream as a whole. Many people point to Bret Victor's demos as a reminder of what's been lost: the program as a live, malleable system you work inside, not text you edit and then run.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer:
The biggest missing idea is a **live, image-based environment** where the editor, development tools, and running program share a single persistent runtime. Mainstream editors still treat software as static text files edited outside a separate build-and-run cycle: you change text, recompile, restart the process, and lose live state. By contrast, Smalltalk environments and Lisp machines kept the entire system—code, data, call stacks, and the IDE itself—alive in one inspectable memory image.

Because there was no hard wall between editing and executing, developers could inspect any live object, redefine a method or function mid-execution inside the debugger, and immediately resume without restarting. Just as importantly, the tooling was self-hosting and malleable: you could inspect a button or pane in the editor itself, modify its behavior on the fly, and save the image. While modern editors approximate pieces of this with hot reload, REPLs, and plugins, they still fundamentally manipulate dead text files rather than living, directly inspectable software systems.
